references.text: Jacob describes how he bore the loss of animals that were torn apart by predators and had to replace them himself. This illustrates the practice of bringing evidence for an animal killed by a predator.

The preceding context concerns entrusted property and taking an oath before the Lord when something disappears without witnesses, which forms the background for the rule regarding damage caused by predators.
Amos uses the image of a shepherd rescuing parts of an animal from the lion's mouth as evidence, illustrating the practice of bringing remains as testimony of a predator attack.
Complementary rules: Exodus 22:12 defines the exception for accidental loss (by a predator), while Leviticus 24:18 establishes the main principle of compensation when human fault is involved.
Contrast in responsibility: 21:34 shows liability through negligence (a pit) with partial compensation, while 22:12 shows full exemption from liability due to external force (a predator).
Opposites in responsibility: 21:36 requires full compensation when danger was known (negligence), while 22:12 exempts from compensation in the case of an unforeseen predator attack.
